title: How do we write a big number in standard form?
description: Four large numbers from the book are rewritten with one digit before the point. The point hops left, and the number of hops becomes the power of ten. Keeko doubts that the number of digits is the power of ten.
teaching_notes: One idea: in standard form the power of ten counts the hops of the point, not the digits. Watch for students who use the number of digits as the power and get a number ten times too big.

video_script.why: A big number is easier to read and compare when one digit sits before the point and the power of ten counts the hops.
video_script.substitution: Hop the point left until one digit is in front, count the hops, and use the count as the power of ten.
video_script.anchor: four large numbers from the book and the hops of the point
video_script.wrong_answer: the power of ten is five
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko counts the digits of 59853 and uses 5 as the power. The point hops only 4 places, so the power is 4; using 5 makes the number ten times too big.
video_script.payoff_line: The number of hops of the point is the power of ten

final_answer.value: 5.9853 × 10⁴, 6.595 × 10⁴, 3.43 × 10 to the power 6 and 7.004 × 10 to the power 10
final_answer.spoken: Five point nine eight five three times ten to the power four. Six point five nine five times ten to the power four. Three point four three times ten to the power six. Seven point zero zero four times ten to the power ten.

maths_rules: 65950 = 6.595 × 10⁴ (4 hops; the last zero after the point is dropped)
the slip: 5.9853 × 10⁵ = 598530, ten times too big
